rules: Pull all three reports at annualcreditreport.com and note which bureau is cleanest. Use the Lender Database tab to pick lenders that pull that bureau in your state.

Experian-leaning: Chase, Amex, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, FNBO, PNC, M&T, TD, USAA. TransUnion-leaning: U.S. Bank, Barclays, Synchrony, Navy Federal, Elan, Apple Card. Equifax-leaning: Truist, Citizens, PenFed, DCU, Huntington, KeyBank, Target (TD). All three: Capital One. Applying to one lender from each group keeps any single report from stacking up.

Chase goes first because of 5/24. Then Amex (2 cards per 90 days), then U.S. Bank (dislikes 5+ new accounts in 12 months), then Wells Fargo, then Bank of America, then regionals. Capital One goes last because it hits all three bureaus and most of its business cards report to personal credit.
Use prequalification tools (Capital One, Discover, Amex Apply With Confidence, Upstart, Upgrade, Fundbox, Capital on Tap) to see offers before taking a hard inquiry.
Business credit runs in parallel at every tier
Form the entity, get an EIN and D-U-N-S number, open a business checking account, then add 3 to 5 net-30 vendors. None of this touches personal credit and it supports every later application.
Stated income is still a statement under penalty of law

Low-doc and no-doc mean the lender does not collect tax returns up front. Income and revenue figures must be accurate, and lenders can ask for proof later (Amex financial reviews are the best known example).
Minimum scores are published floors or community estimates. Income, debt-to-income, utilization, account age, recent inquiries and deposits decide the outcome as much as the score.
